title: What Preserves Eigenvalues: Similarity, Transpose, and the Row-Operation Trap
quickIdea: Similar matrices P^-1 A P and the transpose A^T have the same eigenvalues as A; elementary row operations generally do not.
remember: det(P^-1 A P - lambda I) = det(P^-1 (A - lambda I) P) = det(A - lambda I), so similarity preserves the entire characteristic polynomial.
Similar matrices therefore share trace, determinant, rank and eigenvalues, but not eigenvectors.
A^T has the same characteristic polynomial as A, because det(A^T - lambda I) = det(A - lambda I).
Elementary row operations change eigenvalues in general: elimination is safe for solving Ax = 0 and Ax = b, not for finding eigenvalues.
Multiplying one row by k multiplies det A by k, and the eigenvalues move with it.

example.prompt: Compare the eigenvalues of A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and of the matrix obtained by the row operation R2 <- R2 - 3 R1.
example.work: For A, lambda^2 - 5 lambda - 2 = 0, so the eigenvalues are (5 + sqrt33)/2 and (5 - sqrt33)/2, about 5.372 and -0.372. The row operation R2 <- R2 - 3 R1 gives B = [[1,2],[0,-2]], whose eigenvalues are 1 and -2. The trace moved from 5 to -1, so the eigenvalues moved with it; the determinant happens to stay at -2 here, which is a coincidence of this example, not a rule.
example.answer: Row operations change the eigenvalues, which is why elimination must never be used to find them.

gateAngle: GATE tests this as a statement question: which operations leave the eigenvalues, the determinant or the rank unchanged. The recorded GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.37 on row swaps, kept in the Matrices and Determinants topic, is settled by det(B - lambda I) = -det(A - lambda I) after a single swap: the eigenvalues survive and the determinant changes sign.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A has eigenvalues 1, 2, 3. What are the eigenvalues of A^T, and of 2A?
variations.why: Transposition preserves the characteristic polynomial, while scaling by 2 scales the characteristic polynomial's roots by 2, since det(2A - lambda I) = 2^n det(A - (lambda/2) I).

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does similarity preserve the characteristic polynomial?
variations.answer: P^-1 A P - lambda I = P^-1 (A - lambda I) P, and the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants, so det(P^-1) det(A - lambda I) det(P) = det(A - lambda I).
variations.why: The same computation gives the trace and determinant invariance, because those are coefficients of the characteristic polynomial.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: B is obtained from A by swapping two rows. A has trace 6 and determinant 6. What are tr B and det B?
variations.answer: det B = -6, and the eigenvalues of B are the eigenvalues of A.
variations.why: A row swap multiplies the determinant by -1 and multiplies the characteristic polynomial by -1, so the roots are unchanged while det flips sign. The trace need not be preserved: a swap changes which entries sit on the diagonal.

trap.what: Row-reducing a matrix and then reading the eigenvalues off the resulting triangular matrix.
trap.why: Row operations preserve the solution set of Ax = 0 but not the characteristic polynomial, so the triangular matrix has different eigenvalues from the original.
trap.counterexample: A = [[1,2],[3,4]] has eigenvalues about 5.372 and -0.372, while its row-reduced form [[1,2],[0,-2]] has eigenvalues 1 and -2.

check.question: A and B are similar, and A has eigenvalues 2, 2 and 5 with trace 9. What are the eigenvalues and trace of B?
check.explanation: Similarity preserves the characteristic polynomial, so every coefficient is preserved: eigenvalues, trace, determinant and rank all agree.
